title: Microbiology
tagline: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, how they cause disease, diagnosis and antimicrobials
summary: Microorganisms cause much of the world's disease. This course covers the biology of bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, how pathogens cause disease, the human microbiota, laboratory diagnosis, antimicrobial drugs and resistance, and infection prevention and control.
overview: Medical microbiology studies the organisms that cause infection and the ones that live with us harmlessly. It supplies the reasoning behind every request for a culture and every antibiotic prescription: what kind of organism is likely, how it causes harm, how the laboratory can find it, which drugs act on it, and whether treatment is needed at all.

The first five chapters are about the organisms. Bacteria are introduced through their structure, the Gram stain, growth and genetics, and then grouped the way a laboratory report groups them. A chapter on bacterial pathogenesis explains adhesion, invasion, toxins, biofilms and immune evasion. Viruses follow, with their structure, replication strategies, latency and links to cancer. Fungi and parasites are taught through the patients they affect and the life cycles that explain transmission and diagnosis. The microbiota chapter treats the normal flora as a protective ecosystem and explains what happens when antibiotics disturb it.

The last three chapters are about methods and management. Laboratory diagnosis follows a specimen from collection to report: microscopy, culture, susceptibility testing, antigen and molecular tests, serology, and the predictive values that decide what a result means. Antimicrobials covers how drugs work, how resistance arises and spreads, and the principles of stewardship. Infection prevention and control covers transmission routes, standard and transmission-based precautions, decontamination, surveillance and the arithmetic of outbreaks. Immunology is the natural companion to this course, and infectious diseases applies it at the bedside.
outcomes: Relate bacterial structure, especially the Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell envelopes, capsules and spores, to staining, disease and antibiotic choice, and classify the major pathogens by shape, Gram reaction and oxygen requirement.
Explain how bacteria cause disease through adhesion, invasion, immune evasion, exotoxins, endotoxin and biofilms, with a clinical example of each.
Describe virus structure, the Baltimore classification and the steps of viral replication, and use them to explain latency, oncogenic viruses, antigenic variation and antiviral drug targets.
Recognise the clinically important fungi and parasites, the patients they affect and the life-cycle stages used for diagnosis and control.

Explain the functions of the human microbiota, distinguish colonisation from infection, and outline the pathogenesis of Clostridioides difficile infection and the place of faecal microbiota transplantation.

Follow a specimen through the laboratory, interpret Gram stains, cultures, MICs and breakpoints, antigen, PCR and serology results, and calculate predictive values from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence.

Classify antimicrobial drugs by target and spectrum, explain the main resistance mechanisms with clinical examples (MRSA, VRE, ESBL and carbapenemase producers), and apply pharmacodynamic and stewardship principles.
Apply the chain of infection, standard and transmission-based precautions and decontamination principles, and calculate basic and effective reproduction numbers and herd-immunity thresholds.

history.title: Animalcules
history.detail: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek describes tiny living 'animalcules' seen through his single-lens microscopes in water samples, and later in material scraped from his teeth. These are the first recorded observations of bacteria and protozoa.

history.title: Hand washing in the maternity clinic
history.detail: Ignaz Semmelweis, working in Vienna, requires doctors and students to wash their hands in chlorinated lime before examining women in labour. Deaths from puerperal fever on the doctors' ward fall sharply, decades before germ theory could explain why.

history.title: Against spontaneous generation
history.detail: Louis Pasteur publishes his experiments with swan-neck flasks: boiled broth stays sterile as long as dust and microbes cannot reach it. The result supports the germ theory of disease, and Pasteur goes on to develop attenuated vaccines against chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies.

history.title: Antiseptic surgery
history.detail: Joseph Lister, applying Pasteur's ideas in Glasgow, reports treating compound fractures and wounds with carbolic acid. Wound infection and deaths after surgery fall, and antisepsis becomes the basis of modern surgical practice.

history.title: The tubercle bacillus
history.detail: Robert Koch announces that Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes tuberculosis. His laboratory's methods, pure culture on solid media (agar, suggested by Fanny Hesse) and the dish later named after Julius Petri, give bacteriology its techniques, and the criteria now called Koch's postulates link a microbe to a disease.

history.title: The Gram stain
history.detail: Hans Christian Gram publishes a staining method with crystal violet and iodine that divides bacteria into two groups. The Gram-positive and Gram-negative split reflects two kinds of cell envelope and still guides the first choice of antibiotic.

history.title: Filterable agents
history.detail: Martinus Beijerinck shows that the agent of tobacco mosaic disease passes through filters that hold back bacteria and multiplies only in living tissue, confirming and extending Dmitri Ivanovsky's 1892 observation. He calls it a contagium vivum fluidum; it is the first virus described.

history.title: Penicillin
history.detail: Alexander Fleming notices that a Penicillium mould kills staphylococci on a culture plate. Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their Oxford team purify penicillin and show its effect in 1940–41, and wartime industrial production makes it widely available by 1944–45.

history.title: Helicobacter pylori
history.detail: Robin Warren and Barry Marshall culture a spiral bacterium from the human stomach and link it to gastritis and peptic ulcer. Their work, recognised by the 2005 Nobel Prize, overturns the belief that bacteria cannot live in the stomach.

history.title: The Human Microbiome Project
history.detail: The Human Microbiome Project Consortium publishes reference descriptions of the bacteria living at many body sites of healthy adults, using DNA sequencing rather than culture. The normal microbiota becomes a measurable, variable part of human biology.

references.title: Mims' Medical Microbiology and Immunology
references.authors: Richard V. Goering, Hazel M. Dockrell, Mark Zuckerman and Peter L. Chiodini
references.note: Seventh edition. Organised by body system and clinical syndrome rather than organism, which makes it the closest match to how infection presents in a UK medical school.

references.title: Sherris & Ryan's Medical Microbiology
references.note: Eighth edition. A clear organism-by-organism account with strong chapters on pathogenesis and the immune response to infection.

references.title: Medical Microbiology
references.authors: Patrick R. Murray, Ken S. Rosenthal and Michael A. Pfaller
references.note: Ninth edition. Detailed reference for bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, with good summaries of laboratory diagnosis.

references.title: Breakpoint tables for interpretation of MICs and zone diameters
references.authors: European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST)
references.note: Version 15.0, updated every January. The breakpoints used by UK and European laboratories to report organisms as susceptible, susceptible at increased exposure, or resistant.

references.title: Start smart then focus: antimicrobial stewardship toolkit for inpatient care settings
references.note: The English hospital stewardship framework: start appropriate antibiotics promptly, then review the diagnosis and the prescription at 48–72 hours.

references.title: The WHO AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) antibiotic book
references.note: Classifies antibiotics into Access, Watch and Reserve groups and gives evidence-based empirical choices for common infections.

references.title: National infection prevention and control manual for England
references.note: The standard and transmission-based precautions used in English health and care settings; updated regularly.
